classification.tone: Grim, operatic, emotionally charged, and morally intense

evaluation.positioning_hook: A grief-stricken Catholic father hunts the mob family that destroyed his home, only to discover vengeance and absolution are headed for the same bloody altar.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The script has a clear commercial lane: a revenge-driven crime story with a faith-and-family spine, anchored by a father’s grief and a sister’s police pursuit. The audience promise is immediate, though the material is more adult and intensity-forward than broad four-quadrant fare.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands early with the opening massacre, the family connection to the Risaldis, and Jacob’s turn from mourning father to active avenger. The story engine is easy to explain in one breath: a devastated man tracks the family that murdered his own, while his cop sister tries to stop him.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jacob, Jodie, Ethan, and Victor all carry strong emotional positions, and the script gives each of them a distinct moral posture. The characters are most compelling when they collide around grief, loyalty, and justice; a few supporting players function more as pressure points than fully separate engines.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The Catholic framework is not decorative here; confession, adoration, penance, and liturgy are woven into the story’s emotional architecture. The script also commits to a heightened, almost biblical crime-world register that gives it a distinct identity beyond standard revenge-thriller language.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script moves with strong forward charge: the opening atrocity, the alley confrontation, the club escalation, and the final mansion showdown all keep tightening the vise. The alternating pressure between Jacob, Jodie, and Ethan keeps the momentum alive even when the story pauses for grief or confession.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The combination of Catholic ritual, family trauma, and organized-crime reckoning feels fresh and immediately legible. The story’s most memorable move is making spiritual language and criminal violence speak to each other rather than sit in separate lanes.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The Risaldi family hierarchy, the police response, the church spaces, and the civic pressure around the mayor create a textured ecosystem rather than a simple cat-and-mouse setup. The world is specific enough to feel lived in, especially when the church and criminal family mirror each other as institutions.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unmistakable: solemn, violent, devotional, and emotionally overheated, with moments of dark irony and spiritual yearning. The script knows exactly how it wants to sound, from the confession booth to the ballroom to the final liturgical coda.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Beneath the revenge plot is a sustained meditation on guilt, inherited violence, and whether justice can ever be separated from vengeance. The ending’s emphasis on confession, support, and survival suggests more emotional afterlife than the plot alone would imply.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Jacob/Jodie, Ethan/Victor, Ethan/Frankie, and Jacob/Victor all generate distinct dramatic voltage, and the family structure creates multiple collision paths. The script gets a lot of mileage from sibling loyalty, parental domination, and the way each relationship changes under pressure.

casting_characteristics: One child role with meaningful screen time (Marcus, age 11)
Several roles require strong Catholic/working-class family texture

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with a meaningful exterior component
notable_requirements: Police station, docks, alleyway, graveyard, restaurant, apartment, hotel, and press room settings

technical.vfx_details: Primarily atmospheric work: smoke, fire, snow, and a few stylized transitions/montage moments.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunshots, blood effects, body impacts, fire damage, and practical violence in several set pieces.

rights_flags.detail: Come Back by The Five Stairsteps, Let All Mortal Flesh Keep Silent, O Holy Night, 500 Miles by Peter, Paul and Mary, Good Looking by Suki Waterhouse, Clair de Lune, and L’Amour Toujours are specifically named or used in performance/playback.
Celexa is specifically named on screen.
Michelangelo is referenced through The Creation of Adam.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: Premium streaming or theatrical genre-drama lane
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model; strongest fit is festival-to-platform or prestige genre theatrical with streamer afterlife.

cost.note: The footprint is mostly contained, but the club, mansion, docks, church, and fire/snow sequences create a mid-level production package.

cast.note: The script depends on a strong central quartet and several vivid supporting family roles, plus child casting for Marcus and Jay.

location.note: There are many distinct settings, but most are practical contemporary interiors and exteriors rather than large-scale builds.

content.note: The script includes child murder, gun violence, blood, coercion, grief, and sexual assault testimony, which narrows platform and rating options.

rights.note: Multiple named songs, a branded medication, and a named artwork reference all require clearance attention.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Faith is built into the engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The Catholic framework gives the movie a built-in identity that can travel beyond the crime plot, because confession, penance, and grace are dramatized instead of merely referenced. That makes it attractive to prestige buyers and actors who want genre material with spiritual weight and awards-adjacent emotional stakes.
strengths.evidence: Confession booth scenes, adoration chapel scenes, Father Michael’s sermons, and Jacob’s Act of Contrition structure the story.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The family dynamic is the real hook.
strengths.what_it_means: This is not just a revenge thriller; it is a sibling-and-family tragedy where the emotional engine is Jacob and Jodie trying to survive the same wound from opposite sides of the law. That gives the project a strong actor package lane and a clear audience for elevated crime drama.
strengths.evidence: Jacob and Jodie’s repeated confrontations, their grief over Jay, and their final reconciliation in the ballroom.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Victor is a formidable villain role.
strengths.what_it_means: Victor’s authority, cruelty, and theological language create a villain part with real prestige appeal — a patriarch who weaponizes family, faith, and shame in the same breath. That is the kind of role character actors and awards-minded buyers notice immediately.
strengths.evidence: Victor’s ballroom speeches, the photo-ripping sequence, and his final confrontation with Jacob and Ethan.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The script has a strong visual grammar.
strengths.what_it_means: The story keeps returning to images that can sell the movie in a trailer: stained glass, blood-red club lighting, snow, confession booths, graves, and the final empty spaces. That gives the film a memorable visual identity for marketing and a director a clear tonal palette to own.
strengths.evidence: The adoration chapel lighting, the club’s red emergency lights, the snowstorm, and the final empty-location montage.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ensemble creates multiple collision paths.
strengths.what_it_means: Jacob, Jodie, Ethan, Victor, Frankie, Martin, Edward, and Marcus all have relationships that can generate scenes without depending on the same beat twice. That makes the project feel bigger than a simple two-hander and gives producers more packaging flexibility.
strengths.evidence: Jacob/Jodie, Ethan/Victor, Ethan/Frankie, and Victor/Martin all carry separate dramatic pressure.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The ending lands on emotional release, not just body count.
strengths.what_it_means: The final movement resolves through confession, support, and a return to community, which broadens the movie’s aftertaste beyond revenge. That gives buyers a more durable emotional finish and helps the script play as a prestige genre piece rather than a pure exploitation title.
strengths.evidence: Jacob’s confession, Jodie’s embrace, Ethan and Marcus leaving together, and the church/support-group coda.

whats_special.headline: RISALDI is a prestige-leaning crime thriller with a Catholic soul and a family wound at its center. It offers producers a vivid villain, a bruised but playable lead, and a world where confession and vengeance are always one step apart.

lead_characters.name: Jacob Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Male · late 30s to early 40s · Catholic father
lead_characters.hook: Jacob is a grieving, devout, emotionally frayed father whose faith is both his anchor and his excuse for crossing lines he can no longer uncross. He reads as soft-spoken and decent until the pressure of loss turns him into a man who believes justice is something he must personally deliver.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Casey Affleck in Manchester by the Sea crossed with the moral fracture of Denzel in Training Day — a man whose pain lives just under the skin until it becomes action. Actors who want a role that can play quiet devastation, righteous fury, and spiritual collapse in the same frame will chase this.

lead_characters.name: Jodie Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Female · late 30s to early 40s · police officer
lead_characters.hook: Jodie is a work-driven cop who treats the job like a lifeline, but the script keeps revealing how much of that identity is built on unresolved family grief. She is tough, controlled, and deeply wounded, with a sister’s loyalty that keeps colliding with her professional duty.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the emotional command-center space of Jodie Comer in Killing Eve or Amy Adams in Sharp Objects — a woman whose competence is inseparable from her damage. It gives an actress a role that can pivot between procedural authority, sibling intimacy, and raw breakdown without leaving the movie’s center.

lead_characters.name: Ethan Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the family’s moral hinge: principled, anxious, and desperate to believe he can still choose a different life. He carries the tension of a man born into brutality who keeps trying to speak like someone who might still be saved.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of conflicted, conscience-driven role that gave Jesse Plemons in The Power of the Dog or Paul Dano in Prisoners so much traction — a man whose restraint is the performance. Actors who excel at internal pressure and quiet moral panic will see a lot to play here.

lead_characters.name: Victor Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Victor is the patriarch as ideologue: composed, punitive, and terrifyingly certain that control is the same thing as order. He speaks like a judge, behaves like a king, and treats his children as disposable proof of his power.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase lane of Brian Cox in Succession or Anthony Hopkins in The Father — a commanding elder role that can dominate every room by voice, stillness, and menace. Veteran actors looking for a late-career centerpiece with authority, cruelty, and theatrical bite will circle it fast.

lead_characters.name: Frankie Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Frankie is the brother who still wants to believe obedience can keep him safe, even as the family machine keeps grinding him down. He has a softer center than the others, which makes his fear and loyalty especially playable.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of doomed-family role that gave Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Ben Foster in Hell or High Water so much charge — a man trying to stay useful while panic eats him alive. Character actors who can play tenderness under threat will want it.

lead_characters.name: Martin Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Martin is the family’s volatile performer: sadistic, theatrical, and hungry for approval from a father who only rewards cruelty. He is the most outwardly monstrous of the brothers, but the script also lets him register as a damaged son trapped inside the role he performs.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of feral, high-voltage part that gave Jack Gleeson in Game of Thrones or Tom Hardy in Bronson their breakout menace — a character who can turn on a dime from charm to violence. Actors who want a scene-stealing antagonist with operatic energy will chase it.

lead_characters.name: Edward Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Edward is the family’s blunt instrument: physically imposing, brutal, and almost wordless in the way he carries out orders. He is less expressive than the others, which makes his violence feel even more chilling and efficient.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the strong-silent enforcer slot that actors like Dave Bautista in Blade Runner 2049 or Michael Mando in Better Call Saul have made memorable — a role where physical presence does the storytelling. It gives a performer a chance to build menace through restraint rather than speeches.

lead_characters.name: Alicia Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Alicia is the wife who has spent years surviving inside Victor’s system, and the script makes her quietness feel like a survival skill rather than passivity. She carries shame, fear, and a buried history that gives her scenes a painful stillness.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of bruised, subjugated matriarch role that gave Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects or Frances McDormand in Three Billboards so much texture — a woman whose silence is loaded. Character actresses who can suggest a whole life in a glance will respond to it.

lead_characters.name: Father Michael
lead_characters.hook: Father Michael is the story’s spiritual counterweight: warm, articulate, and unafraid to speak in parable, but never sentimental about suffering. He functions as both pastor and moral interpreter, giving the movie its clearest language for grace.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of wise-but-human clergy role that gave Brendan Gleeson in Calvary or Mark Rylance in The Outfit real authority — a man whose calm carries the movie’s conscience. Actors with gravitas and warmth will be drawn to the sermon scenes and confession-room intimacy.

lead_characters.name: Marcus Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Marcus is the family’s “pure” child, the one Victor fetishizes as innocence and therefore as property. He is quiet, observant, and emotionally exposed, which makes him feel like the last human thing inside the house.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of child role that gives a young actor a haunting, memorable presence without needing pages of dialogue — the emotional function of the boy in The Road or the child in The Banshees of Inisherin’s quieter beats. Casting directors will notice it because the role carries symbolic weight and real vulnerability.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Owens
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Owens is grounded, compassionate, and professional, but she is also the first person to challenge Jacob’s self-destruction without flinching. She gives the movie a modern therapeutic counterpoint to the church’s spiritual one.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the grounded-support role that gives an actor the same kind of steady authority as Jennifer Ehle in Zero Dark Thirty or Cherry Jones in Succession — a listener who can still steer the scene. It’s a strong fit for actors who specialize in calm intelligence and emotional precision.

lead_characters.name: Officer Daniels
lead_characters.hook: Officer Daniels is the cop who sees Jodie’s unraveling before she says it out loud, and he functions as a humane pressure valve inside the station. He’s grizzled, practical, and quietly loyal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the dependable-lieutenant slot that gave Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire or Walton Goggins in Justified so much utility — a working cop with personality and edge. Character actors who can play empathy without softness will like it.

lead_characters.name: Captain Ricks
lead_characters.hook: Captain Ricks is the exhausted institutional face of the case, trying to keep the machine moving while the city burns around him. He reads as a man who knows the scale of the mess but can only manage the next order.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the weary-command role that gives actors the same kind of institutional gravitas as Jeffrey Wright in The Batman or J.K. Simmons in Whiplash — a boss who carries pressure in every line. It’s a strong fit for performers who can make bureaucracy feel dramatic.

lead_characters.name: Chief Pitts
lead_characters.hook: Chief Pitts is the older lawman who still believes leadership means apology, restraint, and trying to do right by the people under him. He gives the police side a moral center that contrasts with the mayor’s opportunism.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of seasoned authority role that gave Ed Harris in Westworld or Richard Jenkins in The Visitor such dignity — a man whose decency is visible in how he speaks to the wounded. Veteran character actors will see a clean, playable lane.

lead_characters.name: Mayor Adams
lead_characters.hook: Mayor Adams is polished, political, and always performing concern for the cameras. He represents the civic layer of the story’s corruption, where image management matters more than truth.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the public-facing power role that gives an actor the same kind of slippery charm as Paul Sparks in House of Cards or Bradley Whitford in Get Out — a man who can smile while the city collapses. It’s ideal for actors who can weaponize charisma.

lead_characters.name: Xavier Winters
lead_characters.hook: Xavier is the husband who has tried to build a normal life around Lucy’s trauma, and his gentleness makes the scene feel lived-in rather than schematic. He’s a quiet witness to the damage without becoming its center.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the understated domestic-support role that gives an actor the same kind of grounded humanity as Scoot McNairy in A Quiet Place Part II or Ben Mendelsohn in many family dramas — a man who makes a scene feel real by listening. It’s a good fit for actors who specialize in naturalism.

lead_characters.name: Lucy Winters
lead_characters.hook: Lucy is a survivor who has rebuilt her life around a hard-won calm, and the script lets her speak with the clarity of someone who has already outlived fear. She is one of the movie’s clearest embodiments of endurance and moral refusal.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the survivor-monologue territory of Jodie Comer in The Last Duel or Elisabeth Moss in The Handmaid’s Tale — a woman who has lived through violation and now speaks with earned force. Actors looking for a contained but devastating testimony scene will want it.

lead_characters.name: Daniel
lead_characters.hook: Daniel is the child who gives Lucy’s survival a future-facing shape, and his presence quietly reframes the scene around chosen family and protection. He is brief but emotionally important.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a small but meaningful child role that gives a young performer a warm, memorable beat in a story full of darkness. Casting teams often look for exactly this kind of clean, emotionally legible child part.

director_appeal.hook: A director who wants to stage faith, violence, and family collapse with operatic seriousness.
director_appeal.fit_profile: Established indie or prestige-genre directors with at least one feature behind them, especially those who already work in performance-forward crime drama, religious imagery, or morally charged thrillers. This material rewards directors who care about blocking, ritual, and emotional escalation more than spectacle for its own sake.
director_appeal.detail: The movie gives a director a rare chance to make confession booths, church aisles, and family dining rooms feel as charged as a shootout. It also offers a clean visual spine — stained glass, snow, blood-red club light, and empty rooms — that a director can turn into a signature.

buyer_appeal.lane: Prestige crime thriller / elevated genre drama
buyer_appeal.detail: The project can be packaged around one strong lead, one strong villain, and a contained ensemble rather than a large star stack, which helps it travel on script and director attachment. The faith-driven crime lane has clear streamer and festival appeal, and the contemporary footprint keeps it exportable without period overhead.

considerations.area: The opening is built as a prologue.
considerations.detail: The first 15 pages function like a separate emotional and narrative block before the main story fully locks in. A next pass could consider how quickly the central engine — Jacob/Jodie/Ethan versus Victor — can be foregrounded so the feature momentum starts even earlier.

considerations.area: The music cues are doing heavy lifting.
considerations.detail: Several named songs are woven into the emotional architecture, and the script clearly uses them as memory triggers and tonal markers. A practical pass would be to protect the same emotional beats while simplifying or consolidating the number of clearance-dependent cues.

considerations.area: The location count is spread across the city.
considerations.detail: The story moves through church spaces, the mansion, the club, the docks, the station, the hotel, the apartment, the graveyard, and multiple exteriors. The version of the script where a few of those spaces are doubled up or absorbed into one another would preserve the escalation while making the production footprint more efficient.

considerations.area: Jodie’s station scenes carry a lot of information.
considerations.detail: The briefing-room and interrogation material does important work, but several of those exchanges repeat the same emotional position around grief, duty, and institutional frustration. One direction would be to let a single scene do more of the work by combining the emotional turn with the procedural turn.

considerations.area: Victor’s ideology is strongest when dramatized.
considerations.detail: His speeches about authority, purity, and meaning are memorable, and the photo-ripping sequence is especially vivid because the belief system becomes physical. A next pass could keep leaning into that kind of action-based expression of character, because it makes the villain feel cinematic rather than merely declarative.

considerations.area: The final movement is emotionally rich.
considerations.detail: The ending gives the movie a strong spiritual landing, but it also carries a lot of reconciliation, coda, and aftermath in a short span. The version of the ending where one emotional beat is allowed to breathe a little longer would protect the catharsis and give the audience more room to land.
